## Summary

- New `GET /api/v1/me/recap` endpoint returning per-agent rollups (checkpoints, tokens, transcript tokens, files changed, labels, skills, MCP servers, tool mix) for the authenticated user, plus an optional `contributors` counterpart aggregated across every contributor on a scoped repo.
- Replaces three separate CLI calls (`GET /me/checkpoints` + `POST /checkpoints/analyses/batch` + `GET /:org/:repo/overview/*`) with one aggregate.
- Powers the "you vs. team" columns in `entire recap` (CLI side: entireio/cli#1015).

## Behavior

- **`?repo=org/name`** — when supplied, both me-side and team-side queries scope to that repo at the SQL level. The response's `contributors` field (top-level + per-agent) carries the team aggregate.
- **No `?repo=`** — me-side aggregates span every repo the user has checkpoints on; team-side is **skipped** entirely (no coherent "everyone else" reference frame across repos), and `contributors` is `null`.
- **`?since=…&until=…`** — ISO-8601 explicit window, takes precedence over `timeframe`. The CLI uses this so `--day`/`--week`/`--month` line up exactly with the server aggregation window.
- **`?timeframe=last-month|last-3-months|last-6-months`** — fallback when explicit dates are absent.

## Implementation

This PR matches the pattern established by /me/activity (#1590): route handler in `api/src/routes/recap.ts` fetches checkpoints + analyses and aggregates qualitative fields (labels/skills/MCP/tool-mix) in JS via `mergeAnalysesInto`. ~1,500 lines, including tests + codegen output.

**The perf refactor — denormalizing those qualitative fields into SQL-aggregatable tables — lives in #1737, stacked on this PR.** Splitting keeps each review focused: this one is "add the endpoint," #1737 is "make it fast." Both should land before the rollout completes.

## Pairs with

- CLI side: entireio/cli#1015
- Perf follow-up: #1737

## Test plan

- [x] Live smoke vs. local wrangler dev (pointed at staging PlanetScale): `GET /api/v1/me/recap?repo=entireio/cli&since=…&until=…` returns populated agents with labels / skills / toolMix.
- [x] `entire recap --view both --insecure-http-auth` (CLI #1015) renders against this endpoint end-to-end.
- [x] `pnpm --filter entire-api run typecheck` — clean.
- [x] `pnpm --filter entire-api run test:run` — all tests passing.
- [x] `pnpm format:check` + `pnpm -r run lint` — clean.

## Out of scope (handled in #1737)

- Denormalized `repo_checkpoint_analysis_labels` / `_skills` / `_tool_mix` / `_mcp` tables
- Worker write path that populates them
- Backfill script for existing analyses
- SQL `GROUP BY` aggregator replacing `mergeAnalysesInto`
- `transcript_tokens` and `files_changed` scalar columns on `repo_checkpoint_analyses`

Follow-up to #1604. Moves /me/recap qualitative aggregates (labels, skills, MCP servers, tool-mix, transcript tokens, files changed) out of `analysis_json` blobs and into denormalized side tables so the route can `GROUP BY` in SQL instead of fetching 1000+ rows of full JSON blobs and aggregating in JS.

## Why

#1604 ships /me/recap matching the /me/activity pattern (fetch checkpoints + analyses, aggregate in JS). Production-equivalent perf measurements showed `--90` recap took 2-5s (estimated) / 60s+ on local wrangler dev — the workerd ↔ Node JSON serialization boundary doesn't scale linearly with row count, and we're shipping ~1000 analysis_json blobs per request.

This PR replaces that with SQL `GROUP BY` against four small denormalized facet tables. Aggregate response size drops from ~1KB-1MB of nested JSON to 5-10 rows of `(name, count)` aggregates per qualitative dimension.

## Architecture

**Schema** — four new tables, identical shape, `(repo_id, checkpoint_id, name, count)` with composite PK and a `(repo_id, name)` index for cross-checkpoint aggregation:
- \`repo_checkpoint_analysis_labels\`
- \`repo_checkpoint_analysis_skills\`
- \`repo_checkpoint_analysis_tool_mix\`
- \`repo_checkpoint_analysis_mcp\`

Plus two new columns on \`repo_checkpoint_analyses\` for scalar aggregates: \`transcript_tokens\` and \`files_changed\`.

**Write path** — analysis-queue worker (\`generateAndStoreReview\`) writes facet rows + scalar columns immediately after \`markComplete\` succeeds. Idempotent under retries (DELETE-then-INSERT inside a transaction).

**Read path** — \`db.analyses.aggregateFacetsByAgent\` does per-agent fan-out: 4 parallel facet aggregates + 1 parallel scalar SUM per agent, all via \`Promise.all\`. Replaces the JS-side \`mergeAnalysesInto\` loop in \`recap.ts\`.

**Backfill** — one-off cursor-paginated script (\`scripts/backfill-analysis-facets.ts\`) that reads existing \`repo_checkpoint_analyses.analysis_json\` rows, parses each blob, and upserts the derived rows. Idempotent. Supports \`--dry-run\` and \`--limit=N\`.

**Feature flag** — \`USE_FACET_AGGREGATOR=true\` (default) routes through SQL aggregation; \`=false\` falls back to legacy \`mergeAnalysesInto\`. Kept for 24h post-deploy as a fast-rollback escape hatch, removed in a follow-up.

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived simplicity.
</HARD-GATE>

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple" projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer visual companion** (if topic will involve visual questions) — this is its own message, not combined with a clarifying question. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec review loop** — dispatch spec-document-reviewer subagent with precisely crafted review context (never your session history); fix issues and re-dispatch until approved (max 5 iterations, then surface to human)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Visual questions ahead?" [shape=diamond];
    "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec review loop" [shape=box];
    "Spec review passed?" [shape=diamond];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];

    "Explore project context" -> "Visual questions ahead?";
    "Visual questions ahead?" -> "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" [label="yes"];
    "Visual questions ahead?" -> "Ask clarifying questions" [label="no"];
    "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec review loop";
    "Spec review loop" -> "Spec review passed?";
    "Spec review passed?" -> "Spec review loop" [label="issues found,\nfix and re-dispatch"];
    "Spec review passed?" -> "User reviews spec?" [label="approved"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**The terminal state is invoking writing-plans.** Do NOT invoke frontend-design, mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. The ONLY skill you invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans.

## The Process

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Review Loop:**
After writing the spec document:

1. Dispatch spec-document-reviewer subagent (see spec-document-reviewer-prompt.md)
2. If Issues Found: fix, re-dispatch, repeat until Approved
3. If loop exceeds 5 iterations, surface to human for guidance

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Key Principles

- **One question at a time** - Don't overwhelm with multiple questions
- **Multiple choice preferred** - Easier to answer than open-ended when possible
- **YAGNI ruthlessly** - Remove unnecessary features from all designs
- **Explore alternatives** - Always propose 2-3 approaches before settling
- **Incremental validation** - Present design, get approval before moving on
- **Be flexible** - Go back and clarify when something doesn't make sense

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion:** When you anticipate that upcoming questions will involve visual content (mockups, layouts, diagrams), offer it once for consent:
> "Some of what we're working on might be easier to explain if I can show it to you in a web browser. I can put together mockups, diagrams, comparisons, and other visuals as we go. This feature is still new and can be token-intensive. Want to try it? (Requires opening a local URL)"

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Do not combine it with clarifying questions, context summaries, or any other content. The message should contain ONLY the offer above and nothing else. Wait for the user's response before continuing. If they decline, proceed with text-only brainstorming.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

# Part 1: Agent coverage — what I found

## CLI side (#1015) is agent-agnostic ✓

The CLI never filters by agent name. `MeFromMeRecap` iterates `resp.Agents` (a generic `map[string]AgentEntry`) and applies the same merge regardless of key. Tests cover `Codex` alongside `Claude Code`. Rendering in `agents_card.go` / `recap_view.go` has no Claude-specific branch. **The CLI faithfully shows whatever the API returns.**

## API analysis pipeline is shaped around Claude tool names

The actual problem lives in `api/src/lib/analysis-queue.ts:extractToolMetrics`. It categorizes tools by hardcoded Claude tool names:

| Tool name | Bucket |
|---|---|
| `Bash` | shell |
| `Read`, `Write`, `Edit` | fileOps |
| `Grep`, `Glob` | search |
| `Agent`, `Skill` | agent |
| `mcp__*` prefix | mcp |
| anything else | other |

For non-Claude agents:
- **Codex** emits `bash`, `apply_patch` → all land in `other`
- **Cursor** has its own tool naming → mostly `other`
- **OpenCode**, **FactoryAI Droid**, **Copilot CLI**, **Gemini** → similar
- **Skills** counter only fires on Claude's `Skill` tool — so non-Claude skill arrays are always empty
- **MCP servers** detection depends on the `mcp__*` prefix (Claude convention) — so non-Claude MCP usage isn't surfaced
- **Labels** come from a separate LLM extraction on chunked transcript text — *those* should work for any agent

There's a unified transcript parser layer (`api/src/lib/transcript-parsers/`) with parsers for each agent that normalizes the loading side. The categorization step downstream of it didn't get the same treatment.

**So what you're seeing in your recap is a real coverage gap, not a bug in #1015 or in the new endpoint.** It's been this way since the analysis pipeline shipped.

The fix lives on the API side — generalize `extractToolMetrics` to consume normalized tool taxonomies instead of raw Claude tool names. That's its own piece of work, separate from the recap endpoint.

---

# Part 2: Brainstorming — what I'd do differently if redoing #1015

Before I propose ideas, I want to understand which dimension you're most interested in exploring. The CLI recap codebase is ~6k lines split across ~30 files (rendering, model, view, cache, aggregation, network, TUI). A "what would you do differently" answer can mean very different things depending on which axis matters most to you.

**Which of these matters most for the brainstorm?** (you can pick more than one)

1. **Code structure** — file boundaries, package layout, what belongs where (the 6k lines feel sprawly)
2. **Data flow** — how local-CLI data, server data, and the rendering layer hand off (currently the network-fetched data overrides local in a few places via `applyServerMe`, which is hard to reason about)
3. **Styling / TUI architecture** — how the view-with-filters interacts with the model, how scroll/refresh/redraw work
4. **Cross-agent handling end-to-end** — given the gap I just described, design a recap that properly supports any agent without Claude-shaped assumptions baked in
5. **Test architecture** — there's a `testutil_test.go` at 302 lines, lots of test files; could be tighter
6. **Something else** you've been bothered by

Which axis (or axes) do you want to dig into?

# Answer for that specific Codex commit

I traced commit `a9e6e67b6e74ef97a632799691bb0266be19fdf9` — checkpoint ID `7a9387cf9003`, agent `Codex`, model `gpt-5.5`.

The transcript is in **Codex's native format** (`type: session_meta`, `type: event_msg`, etc.) — not Claude's `type: "assistant"` + `content[].type: "tool_use"`. There are two analysis paths and they handle this very differently.

## What gets produced for Codex (per checkpoint analysis)

| Field | Source | Codex result | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `labels` | LLM analysis on chunked transcript text | ✅ **Works** | Goes through `buildSessionsFromStrippedTranscript` → `getParserForAgent("Codex")` → unified parser. Transcript content reaches the LLM as normalized messages. |
| `transcriptTokens` | Session metadata `token_usage` | ✅ **Works** | Pulled from `metadata.json`'s `token_usage` block — agent-agnostic. |
| `filesChanged` | Commit data | ✅ **Works** | From `repo_commits.files_changed`, has nothing to do with the transcript shape. |
| `toolMix` (shell/fileOps/search/mcp/agent/other) | `extractToolMetrics` raw-JSONL scan | ❌ **All zero** | Filters lines on `parsed.type === "assistant"` — Codex never emits that. |
| `skillsUsed` | `extractToolMetrics` `Skill` tool detection | ❌ **Empty** | Skills counter only fires on Claude's `Skill` tool with `input.skill`. |
| `mcpServersUsed` | `extractToolMetrics` `mcp__*` prefix scan | ❌ **Empty** | Only Claude's tool naming uses the `mcp__server__tool` prefix convention. |

## Where the gap lives in code

```
api/src/lib/analysis-queue.ts:extractToolMetrics  ← Claude-shaped, 0 tool counts for Codex
api/src/lib/checkpoint-transcript.ts:buildSessions ← Uses unified parser, agent-aware ✓
api/src/lib/checkpoint-analysis-pipeline.ts:generateCheckpointAnalysis ← Uses parsed content ✓
```

The parsing layer already has `cursor-parser.ts`, `codex-parser.ts`, `opencode-parser.ts`, `droid-parser.ts`, `copilot-cli-parser.ts`, `gemini-parser.ts`, `kiro-parser.ts`, `pi-parser.ts` — full coverage.

But `extractToolMetrics` reads the raw JSONL string and never goes through any of those parsers. The function was written when only Claude shipped, then never updated when other agents landed.

## What this means in your recap output for that Codex commit

- **Codex card shows real labels** (e.g., `bug_fix` for that redact commit) — that flows through correctly
- **Token total shows real value** — the 71k/8k/2.5M cache numbers are there
- **Files changed shows real count**
- **Skills row is empty** — even if you used Codex skills, they don't surface
- **MCP servers row is empty** — same reason
- **Tool mix bar is all zeros** — shell/fileOps/etc all read 0 for Codex

That's why you're seeing the asymmetry. Not "no data for non-Claude" but "half the data for non-Claude" — and the half that's missing is the visually loud half (the tool-mix bar and the skills/MCP rows).

## How to fix

The right fix is on the API side: route `extractToolMetrics` through the unified parser like the labels path already does. Each agent parser would expose normalized "tool calls" via the parser interface, and `extractToolMetrics` would consume normalized events instead of raw Claude-shaped JSONL. Roughly:

1. Add a `getToolCalls()` method to each agent parser returning `Array<{ name, category, input? }>`
2. Each parser maps its native tool naming to the shared `shell|fileOps|search|mcp|agent|other` taxonomy
3. `extractToolMetrics` calls `parser.getToolCalls()` instead of scanning JSONL

That's a separate piece of work from the recap endpoint — it's an analysis-pipeline fix that retroactively benefits every recap. Worth its own PR.

---

# Now back to part 2 — brainstorming

I asked which dimension you wanted to focus on for "what would I do differently on #1015". Given the Codex coverage discovery just now, I think dimension #4 (cross-agent handling end-to-end) might be the most natural lens — it's the one that surfaces the kind of structural assumption we just found.

But you tell me. **Which axis (or axes) do you want to explore?**

1. **Code structure** — file boundaries, package layout
2. **Data flow** — local vs server data merge (`applyServerMe`)
3. **Styling / TUI architecture** — view/model/scroll/redraw
4. **Cross-agent handling end-to-end** — design assuming multi-agent from day 1
5. **Test architecture**
6. Something else

{"body":"## Summary

Adds `entire review` — a command that runs configured review skills (e.g. `/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr`, `/codex:adversarial-review`) inside an agent session, tags that session as a review, and permanently attaches review metadata to the next checkpoint on commit. Tracking-first: no custom review prompts, just wraps existing skills so reviewers don't redundantly re-run them on the same commit.

Three workflows, one command:
- **Author self-review**: `entire review` → agent runs skills → commit → next reviewer sees `HasReview=true` and can skip.
- **Designated reviewer**: same flow, different seat.
- **One-shot feedback**: `entire review` → stop after the review, no commit needed.

No new trailers, no finalize step, no empty commits. The review session rides the normal checkpoint condensation pipeline; `kind: "agent_review"` on `CommittedMetadata` and `has_review: true` on `CheckpointSummary` are the only new persisted data.

## What's in this PR

**Command surface (`review.go`)**
- `entire review` — load config, spawn configured agent, show scope summary
- `entire review --edit` — interactive `huh` picker for per-agent skills (pre-checks saved choices, alphabetical agent order, `[i/N]` counter)
- `entire review --track-only` — write the pending marker without spawning (for manual start)

**Scoping**
- `Reviewing feat/X vs main: 3 commits, 7 files changed, 2 uncommitted` printed before launch (falls back gracefully on detached HEAD / clean default branch)
- `detectBaseBranch`: `origin/HEAD` → `origin/main` → `origin/master` → local main/master
- Re-run guard: reads `HasReview` from the checkpoint summary via `ResolveCommittedReaderForCheckpoint` (v1 + v2 aware), prompts before re-reviewing HEAD

**Pending-marker handshake (`lifecycle.go`)**
- `.git/entire-sessions/review-pending.json` written by `entire review`, adopted by the spawned agent's first `UserPromptSubmit` hook, cleared on adoption
- Worktree-scoped: a session in another worktree of the same repo won't race to claim the marker
- Deferred best-effort cleanup so an agent quitting before `UserPromptSubmit` doesn't leave a stale marker

**Checkpoint metadata (`checkpoint/`, `strategy/manual_commit_condensation.go`)**
- `WriteCommittedOptions.Kind` + `ReviewSkills` + `HasReview` populated by condensation
- `CheckpointSummary.HasReview` is an umbrella flag — future review kinds (e.g. manual review) should also set it, no new boolean needed
- `session.Kind.IsReview()` is the single source of truth for the umbrella; checkpoint package uses `opts.HasReview` directly (no string coupling)

**Agent launching (`agent/agent.go`, per-agent `claude.go` / `codex.go` / `gemini.go`)**
- New `Launcher` interface with `LaunchCmd(ctx, prompt) (*exec.Cmd, error)`
- Subprocess-spawn implementations for Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI
- `agent.LauncherFor(name)` returns the launcher or `ok=false` (falls back to `--track-only` with a manual instruction)

**Settings (`settings/settings.go`)**
- `EntireSettings.Review` is `map[string][]string` (agent → skill list)
- Load errors are surfaced to the user (malformed JSON no longer wipes the file when the picker runs)

**Status (`status.go`)**
- `Review · reviewed (checkpoint abc123…)` line when HEAD's checkpoint has `HasReview`

## Test plan

- [x] `mise run check` — fmt + lint + unit + integration + Vogon E2E canary, all green
- [x] Local `golangci-lint run` (CI-mode, no `--fix`): 0 issues
- [x] Manual smoke on `~/demo-repository`: `entire review` → Claude opens with composed prompt → session tagged `kind: "agent_review"` with full `review_skills` list → worktree scoping verified (my own session in `.worktrees/entire-review` did NOT steal the marker)
- [x] `entire review --track-only` verified to write marker with `worktree_path` field populated
- [ ] Real agent E2E exercising the full loop (marker → adoption → commit → HasReview=true on summary) — deferred to a follow-up

## Review feedback addressed on this PR

The following findings from Cursor Bugbot / Copilot / multi-agent PR review pass were fixed during review iteration:
- Review checkpoint lookup for v2 stores (was v1-only)
- `detectBaseBranch` fallback chain (doc said one thing, code did another — twice, both fixed + pinned by test)
- Pending marker could survive a clean agent exit without `UserPromptSubmit` — now has deferred cleanup
- `saveReviewConfig` + `runReview` no longer wipe user settings on parse error
- `HasReview` derivation no longer string-coupled to `session.KindAgentReview` across a package boundary

## Follow-up (not blocking)

- Integration/E2E exercising the full review-session → condensation → HasReview loop

- Surface `ReviewSkills` in `entire explain` output

{"body":"## Summary

Adds a multi-agent mode to `entire review`. When multiple eligible agents support headless execution, the CLI multi-selects agents, prompts for optional per-run context, runs N reviews in parallel with a Bubble Tea status table, and (optionally) synthesizes a unified cross-agent verdict at the end.

Closes Phase 2 of the `entire review` redesign (items 1–4) on top of PR #993 / #1009. Phase 1 (install-aware skill picker) shipped separately.

## Phase 2 — what landed

### 1. Pick the review agent
- Spawn-time picker when 2+ agents are configured (`81c4c1192`).
- Per-run prompt textarea after agent selection so users can scope a single run without editing settings (`434a6ae96`).

### 2. Parallel headless spawn + status table
- New `agent.HeadlessLauncher` capability interface; per-agent implementations for claude-code, codex, gemini-cli (`b53d82f1e`).
- Binary lookup deferred to `Cmd.Start` so construction is infallible and unit tests verify argv/stdin contracts without the agent binaries on PATH (`880bae867`).
- Codex / gemini headless invocation + Ctrl+C cancellation cascade with a 5s SIGKILL watchdog (`8e82e407a`).
- `multiReviewOrchestrator` runs N agents in parallel under a shared cancellation context, owns the pending-review marker lifecycle, and dumps per-agent results once the TUI exits (`b0036d737`).
- `reviewTUIModel` (Bubble Tea) renders a live status table with spinner, per-row duration, token count, and a faint preview line (`701bf3948`).
- Codex exec-mode noise filter strips session chrome (banners, hook firings, `exec ...` blocks, timestamped errors) before the per-agent dump so findings aren't buried (`d0f05d1bd`).

### 3. Ctrl+O drill-in + aggregated dumps
- Press Ctrl+O during a run to drill into any agent's live buffer; ←/→ to switch agents, Esc to return (`21920e4f5`). Drill-in uses the alt-screen so the table doesn't tear underneath (`b2466e5c0`).
- After all agents finish, the orchestrator emits one `─────── <agent> review ───────` block per agent containing the filtered narrative.

### 4. AI-synthesized cross-agent verdict
- New opt-in (`y/N`) prompt after the per-agent dumps. Reuses `resolveCheckpointSummaryProvider` (the same picker `entire explain` uses) to resolve a configured summary agent and asks it to produce a unified verdict with sections for common findings, unique findings, disagreements, and priority order (`840239d32`).
- Skipped silently when stdin isn't a TTY, when the run was cancelled, or when fewer than two agents produced usable output. Provider failures degrade to a one-line "synthesis unavailable" notice — the user can still commit the underlying reviews.

## Other improvements

- **Per-agent marker entries.** Multi-agent markers carry a per-agent map of `{Skills, Prompt}` so each adopting hook records the skills/prompt that *that* agent actually ran. ## What #1737's perf fix did

`#1737` made the **read** fast:
- Before: route fetched `analysis_json` blobs and aggregated in JS (60s+)
- After: route runs `GROUP BY` against denormalized facet tables (~1s)

The data getting read is the same data — just laid out differently in storage so SQL can aggregate it without parsing JSON.

## What's actually wrong for non-Claude agents

The **producer** of that data — `extractToolMetrics` — has been Claude-shaped from day 1. So when a Codex checkpoint runs through the pipeline today:

```
Codex transcript (event_msg, session_meta, ...)
    ↓
extractToolMetrics — looks for `type === "assistant"` → finds nothing
    ↓
analysis_json written with: toolMix={shell:0, fileOps:0, ...}, skills=[], mcpServers=[]
    ↓
Worker writes facet tables from that analysis_json
    ↓
Facet tables for that checkpoint: empty for tool_mix/skills/mcp
    ↓
Recap reads facet tables → returns empty
```

So the rows in production *today* — for every Codex/Cursor/Gemini/etc checkpoint that's already been analyzed — have **wrong (zero) data baked in** at every layer: in `analysis_json`, in the facet tables. The faster read path reads the same wrong data faster.

## What "fixing the parser" does

If I fix `extractToolMetrics` to use each agent's parser:
- **Going forward:** every new Codex checkpoint produces correct `analysis_json` and correct facet rows. Their recap shows real toolMix/skills/mcp.
- **Going backward (existing rows):** nothing changes automatically. The bad zeros in `analysis_json` and facet tables stay. Recap for those old commits stays empty.

## Why "backfill" comes up

The question is: do you want the existing thousands of Codex/Cursor/Gemini checkpoints to *retroactively* show correct toolMix/skills, or do you accept that:
- Anything from before the fix → blank toolMix
- Anything after the fix → real toolMix
- Over time, as new checkpoints accumulate, the gap fades naturally

That's the choice. **Backfill = re-extract from existing transcripts to fix old rows.** No backfill = old rows stay wrong.

## My recommendation: no backfill

For your specific question — looking at your *Codex commit yesterday* — the parser fix doesn't change anything for that commit retroactively unless we backfill. But:
- Backfill of just toolMix/skills/mcp (option C — re-extract from transcripts without re-running the LLM) is a one-shot script similar to the existing `backfill-analysis-facets.ts`. Maybe ~150 lines.
- Re-running full analysis (option B — burn tokens for re-analysis) is the wrong answer because labels are already correct; only the deterministic post-extraction is wrong.

So the real question is: do you want a one-shot script that re-extracts toolMix from existing `analysis_json` transcripts and updates the facet tables for non-Claude checkpoints? Or accept they stay empty and wait for the data to age out as new checkpoints accumulate?

If your honest answer is "I want my recap to show correct data for the work I did yesterday on Codex" — then yes, we need a small backfill script as part of the parser-fix PR. If your answer is "the 24-hour soak window is fine and I don't mind old data being slightly off" — then no backfill needed.

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** This should be run in a dedicated worktree (created by brainstorming skill).

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (if subagents available) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## Remember
- Exact file paths always
- Complete code in plan (not "add validation")
- Exact commands with expected output
- Reference relevant skills with @ syntax
- DRY, YAGNI, TDD, frequent commits

## Plan Review Loop

After completing each chunk of the plan:

1. Dispatch plan-document-reviewer subagent (see plan-document-reviewer-prompt.md) with precisely crafted review context — never your session history. This keeps the reviewer focused on the plan, not your thought process.
   - Provide: chunk content, path to spec document

3. If ✅ Approved: proceed to next chunk (or execution handoff if last chunk)

**Chunk boundaries:** Use `## Chunk N: <name>` headings to delimit chunks. Each chunk should be ≤1000 lines and logically self-contained.

**Review loop guidance:**
- Same agent that wrote the plan fixes it (preserves context)
- If loop exceeds 5 iterations, surface to human for guidance
- Reviewers are advisory - explain disagreements if you believe feedback is incorrect

After saving the plan:

classifyTool(call: ToolCall): ToolMixCategory {
  const name = call.name
  if (name === "Bash") return "shell"
  if (name === "Read" || name === "Write" || name === "Edit") return "fileOps"
  if (name === "Grep" || name === "Glob") return "search"
  if (name === "Skill" || name === "Agent") return "agent"
  if (name.startsWith("mcp__")) return "mcp"
  return "other"
}

extractSkillFromTool(call: ToolCall): string | null {
  if (call.name !== "Skill") return null
  const skill = (call.input as Record<string, unknown>)?.skill
  return typeof skill === "string" && skill.length > 0 ? skill : null
}

extractMcpServerFromTool(call: ToolCall): string | null {
  if (!call.name.startsWith("mcp__")) return null
  const segments = call.name.split("__")
  return segments.length >= 3 && segments[1] ? segments[1] : null
}

import { getParserForAgent } from "./transcript-parsers/registry"
import { TOOL_MIX_CATEGORY_KEYS } from "../types"

export interface ParsedSessionForMetrics {
  agent: string
  messages: TranscriptMessage[]
}

export function extractToolMetricsFromSessions(sessions: ParsedSessionForMetrics[]): {
  skillsUsed: string[]
  mcpServersUsed: { name: string; count: number }[]
  toolProfile: ToolProfile | null
} {
  const skills = new Set<string>()
  const mcpCounts = new Map<string, number>()
  const counts: Record<ToolMixCategoryKey, number> = {
    shell: 0,
    fileOps: 0,
    search: 0,
    mcp: 0,
    agent: 0,
    other: 0,
  }
  let total = 0

  for (const session of sessions) {
    const parser = getParserForAgent(session.agent)
    for (const message of session.messages) {
      const toolCalls = message.toolCalls ?? []
      for (const call of toolCalls) {
        total++
        const cat = parser.classifyTool?.(call) ?? "other"
        counts[cat]++

        const skill = parser.extractSkillFromTool?.(call)
        if (skill) skills.add(skill)

        const mcpServer = parser.extractMcpServerFromTool?.(call)
        if (mcpServer) {
          mcpCounts.set(mcpServer, (mcpCounts.get(mcpServer) ?? 0) + 1)
        }
      }
    }
  }

  let toolProfile: ToolProfile | null = null
  if (total > 0) {
    const categories = Object.fromEntries(
      TOOL_MIX_CATEGORY_KEYS.map((k) => [k, { count: counts[k] }]),
    ) as Record<ToolMixCategoryKey, { count: number }>
    toolProfile = { categories, total }
  }

  return {
    skillsUsed: Array.from(skills),
    mcpServersUsed: Array.from(mcpCounts.entries())
      .map(([name, count]) => ({ name, count }))
      .sort((a, b) => b.count - a.count),
    toolProfile,
  }
}

/**
 * @deprecated Use extractToolMetricsFromSessions. Kept for two release cycles
 * so any external caller (none in-tree) doesn't break.
 */
export function extractToolMetrics(
  sessionsMap: Record<string, string | StoredTranscriptSession>,
): { skillsUsed: string[]; mcpServersUsed: { name: string; count: number }[]; toolProfile: ToolProfile | null } {
  // Bridge: assume Claude shape (the historical default). New callers should
  // use extractToolMetricsFromSessions with parsed sessions.
  const claudeParser = getParserForAgent("Claude Code")
  const sessions: ParsedSessionForMetrics[] = []
  for (const stored of Object.values(sessionsMap)) {
    const jsonl = typeof stored === "string" ? stored : stored?.content
    if (typeof jsonl !== "string") continue
    sessions.push({ agent: "Claude Code", messages: claudeParser.parse(jsonl).messages })
  }
  return extractToolMetricsFromSessions(sessions)
}
```

Reviewer findings are in. **Chunk 1 approved**, **Chunks 2-5 have real issues** — some critical (would block the implementer), some minor.

## Honest summary of what came back

### Chunk 1 — Approved ✅
Minor recommendations only.

### Chunk 2 — Issues Found ⚠️ (some critical)
- **Wrong Codex tool names.** The reviewer ran my fixture-extraction script against the real Codex transcript and got: `exec_command:221`, `update_plan:4`, `apply_patch:11`, `write_stdin:55`, `_list_pull_request_review_threads:4`, `_fetch_pr_comments:2`. **Not** `bash` / `read_file` like my plan example claimed. With the proposed classifier, ~90% of real Codex calls would land in `other` — barely better than the current bug.
- **Cursor parser doesn't currently emit `toolCalls`** — the classifier I added would be dead code today; needs a parser-change task first or explicit acknowledgment.
- File path inconsistency between the file-structure table and Task 4.
- Task 4's "paste output" instruction should be a shell redirect.

### Chunk 3 — Issues Found ⚠️
- Codex test fixture is a `// … placeholder` comment instead of real lines.
- `loaded.sessions` field shape needs verification (would fail at runtime if wrong).
- Task 9's TDD ordering is contradictory (test passes immediately after Tasks 3-8 are done — there's no failing-test phase to drive it).

### Chunk 4 — Issues Found ⚠️ (most critical)
- **`loadCheckpointTranscript` signature is wrong.** Real signature takes a single object with required `checkpoint`, `checkpointRepoFullName`, `token` fields — not the positional args my plan used. Two of those aren't on the analysis row; the script needs ~5-line prologue per row.
- **The "mirror `backfill-analysis-facets.ts`" guidance fails because that file doesn't exist on `main` yet** — it's only on the `feat/recap-facets-sql-agg` branch (#1737). My plan branches off `main`, so there's no model to copy.
- Idempotency, cursor advancement, sessions-empty check, and JSON merge semantics are all under-specified.
- Task 12 (tests) is ordered after Task 11 (implementation) — inverts TDD.

### Chunk 5 — Issues Found ⚠️
- Pre-push gauntlet uses `test:unit` (curated subset); CI runs full `test:run` against MySQL workers. A test that breaks under the full config but passes under unit would land green locally / red in CI.
- Missing DB-types drift check (CI runs it).
- PR body says "pinned numbers" but Task 10's actual assertion is `total > 0`.

---

## My read on next steps

Two of the issues (Codex tool names, missing model script on `main`) make me question whether the plan's framing is right at all. Specifically:

1. **The Codex classifier needs ~6-7 specific tool names mapped, not the 2-3 I sketched.** That's a research task, not a "implementer fills it in." Worth doing right in the plan since it's load-bearing.

2. **Stacking vs forking.** If we branch off `main`, the backfill script is standalone (no model to mirror). If we stack on `feat/recap-facets-sql-agg` (#1737), we re-use that branch's structure but create another stacked PR. The plan assumed a model existed on `main` — neither option matches that.

3. **Cursor's classifier is currently dead code.** Either the plan adds a Cursor-parser change to surface toolCalls (scope creep), or it explicitly defers Cursor with a comment.

I think the right move is **revise the plan with the critical fixes baked in**, then re-run the reviewer on revised chunks. The minor issues (TDD framing nits, advisory recommendations) can ride along.

Three options for how to proceed:

- **A. Full plan revision.** I rewrite the affected sections (~most of Chunks 2 and 4) and re-run the chunk-by-chunk reviewer. ~30 min before any code is touched.
- **B. Trim the plan and execute looser.** Acknowledge the plan as a sketch; execute task by task with you in the loop on each chunk's specific decisions (tool name list, branching choice, etc.). Less upfront cost, more interactive.
- **C. Drop Chunk 4 (backfill) from this PR entirely.** Ship just Chunks 1-3 (parser fix → producer correctness for new checkpoints). Backfill becomes a follow-up that benefits from the perf branch's actual `runBackfill` model once it merges. Smaller surface, faster shipping.

Honest preference: **C**, then **B**. The backfill is what makes "no users have seen this yet → all data is new" meaningful. But it's the part where the plan went sideways. If we ship just the producer fix first, every NEW checkpoint after merge is correct, and the backfill becomes a focused follow-up against an actual model script.

Which direction?
i think a is probably the best then and most concrete?

54	    if (content) {

## Summary

Recap's per-agent toolMix / skills / mcpServers were Claude-shaped: `extractToolMetrics` scanned raw JSONL for `type === "assistant"` + `mcp__*` prefix + the `Skill` tool. Codex and Gemini transcripts use different shapes, so those agents got all-zero results in the response. This PR replaces the JSONL scan with a per-agent classifier dispatch through the existing transcript-parser layer, and adds a backfill script to correct existing rows.

Cursor's classifier is intentionally **not** in this PR — `cursor-parser.ts` doesn't currently surface `toolCalls` in its parsed output, so a classifier on it would be dead code. Surfacing tool calls in the Cursor parser is a separate piece of work; this PR is structured so adding that classifier later is a one-file change.

## Changes

- New `tool-categories.ts` with `ToolMixCategory` + default classifier
- `TranscriptParser` interface gains three optional methods: `classifyTool`, `extractSkillFromTool`, `extractMcpServerFromTool`
- Classifier implementations on Claude / Codex / Gemini / fallback parsers, with Codex coverage pinned to a captured real-fixture distribution (no zeros for production data)
- `extractToolMetricsFromSessions` replaces `extractToolMetrics` — consumes parsed `TranscriptMessage[]` instead of raw JSONL, dispatches via each session's agent. No backwards-compat bridge; the only in-tree caller (the worker write path) is updated in the same commit.
- New backfill script `scripts/backfill-analysis-tool-metrics.ts` re-runs the extractor against existing transcripts and overwrites only `toolProfile`, `skillsUsed`, `mcpServersUsed` in `analysis_json`. Cursor-paginated, idempotent, supports `--dry-run` and `--limit=N`. **No LLM calls** — labels are already correct.

- #1604 (recap endpoint)
- #1737 (perf via SQL aggregation)

- [x] Backfill script tests: happy-path overwrite preserves unrelated fields, dry-run no-op, `--limit` exact-equality, narrow `SyntaxError` catch with infra-error propagation, no-sessions skip path
EOF
)"

 *
 * Targets `checkpoints-v2-org-{orgName}` — one document per transcript chunk
 * rather than one document per checkpoint. This enables snippet-level search

 *
 * Options:
 *   --repo <full_name>     Only backfill a specific repo (e.g., "entireio/cli")
 *   --repo-id <uuid>       Only backfill a specific repo by its database UUID
 *   --with-transcripts     Fetch full transcripts from GitHub (slower, needs GITHUB_TOKEN)
 *                          Without this flag, only metadata (prompt/commit/files) is indexed.
 *   --dry-run              Show what would be indexed without writing to Turbopuffer
 *   --limit <n>            Max checkpoints per repo (for testing)
 *
 * Environment:
 *   DATABASE_URL           MySQL connection string (defaults to local Docker MySQL)
 *   TURBOPUFFER_API_KEY    Turbopuffer API key (required unless --dry-run)
 *   OPENAI_API_KEY         OpenAI API key for embeddings (required unless --dry-run)
 *   GITHUB_TOKEN           GitHub PAT with repo read access (required for --with-transcripts)
 */

const GITHUB_API = "https://api.github.com"
const TRANSCRIPT_CONCURRENCY = 15 // parallel GitHub API fetches per chunk

     576 api/scripts/backfill-search.ts
---FALLBACK PARSER---
import { ClaudeCodeParser } from "./claude-code-parser"
import type { TranscriptParser, TranscriptParseResult } from "./types"

/**
 * Fallback parser for unknown agents.
 * Delegates to ClaudeCodeParser for best-effort parsing (the Anthropic API
 * message format is common across agents using the checkpoint protocol)
 * but marks the result as a fallback so the frontend can show a warning.
 */
const FALLBACK_WARNING =
  "Full transcript parsing is not yet available for this agent. Some messages or tool calls may not display correctly."

export class FallbackParser implements TranscriptParser {
  readonly name = "Fallback"
  readonly format = "jsonl" as const
  private delegate = new ClaudeCodeParser()

  private asFallback(result: TranscriptParseResult): TranscriptParseResult {
    return { messages: result.messages, isFallback: true, warning: FALLBACK_WARNING }
  }

  parse(jsonlContent: string): TranscriptParseResult {
    return this.asFallback(this.delegate.parse(jsonlContent))
  }

  parseFrom(content: string, offset: number): TranscriptParseResult {
    return this.asFallback(this.delegate.parseFrom(content, offset))
  }
}

**Architecture:** The transcript parsers already normalize each agent's native format into a shared `TranscriptMessage[]` shape carrying `toolCalls?: ToolCall[]`. This plan inverts the dependency: each parser exposes an agent-specific tool classifier as optional methods on the existing `TranscriptParser` interface, and a refactored `extractToolMetricsFromSessions` consumes parser output instead of raw JSONL. import type { ToolMixCategory } from "../../types"
// (ToolCall is already imported)

// inside the class:
classifyTool(call: ToolCall): ToolMixCategory {
  const name = call.name
  if (name === "Bash") return "shell"
  if (name === "Read" || name === "Write" || name === "Edit") return "fileOps"
  if (name === "Grep" || name === "Glob") return "search"
  if (name === "Skill" || name === "Agent") return "agent"
  if (name.startsWith("mcp__")) return "mcp"
  return "other"
}

extractSkillFromTool(call: ToolCall): string | null {
  if (call.name !== "Skill") return null
  const skill = (call.input as Record<string, unknown>)?.skill
  return typeof skill === "string" && skill.length > 0 ? skill : null
}

extractMcpServerFromTool(call: ToolCall): string | null {
  if (!call.name.startsWith("mcp__")) return null
  const segments = call.name.split("__")
  return segments.length >= 3 && segments[1] ? segments[1] : null
}
```

```ts
export interface ParsedSessionForMetrics {
  agent: string
  messages: TranscriptMessage[]
}

export function extractToolMetricsFromSessions(sessions: ParsedSessionForMetrics[]): {
  skillsUsed: string[]
  mcpServersUsed: { name: string; count: number }[]
  toolProfile: ToolProfile | null
} {
  const skills = new Set<string>()
  const mcpCounts = new Map<string, number>()
  const counts: Record<ToolMixCategory, number> = {
    shell: 0,
    fileOps: 0,
    search: 0,
    mcp: 0,
    agent: 0,
    other: 0,
  }
  let total = 0

  for (const session of sessions) {
    const parser = getParserForAgent(session.agent)
    for (const message of session.messages) {
      for (const call of message.toolCalls ?? []) {
        total++
        const cat = parser.classifyTool?.(call) ?? "other"
        counts[cat]++

        const skill = parser.extractSkillFromTool?.(call)
        if (skill) skills.add(skill)

        const mcpServer = parser.extractMcpServerFromTool?.(call)
        if (mcpServer) {
          mcpCounts.set(mcpServer, (mcpCounts.get(mcpServer) ?? 0) + 1)
        }
      }
    }
  }

  let toolProfile: ToolProfile | null = null
  if (total > 0) {
    const categories = Object.fromEntries(
      TOOL_MIX_CATEGORY_KEYS.map((k) => [k, { count: counts[k] }]),
    ) as Record<ToolMixCategory, { count: number }>
    toolProfile = { categories, total }
  }

  return {
    skillsUsed: Array.from(skills),
    mcpServersUsed: Array.from(mcpCounts.entries())
      .map(([name, count]) => ({ name, count }))
      .sort((a, b) => b.count - a.count),
    toolProfile,
  }
}
```

```ts
// api/scripts/backfill-analysis-tool-metrics.ts
#!/usr/bin/env tsx
/**
 * Backfill repo_checkpoint_analyses.analysis_json with corrected toolMix /
 * skills / mcpServers across every agent. Idempotent — safe to re-run.
 *
 * Why: extractToolMetrics was Claude-shaped before fix/agent-aware-tool-metrics.
 * Existing rows have toolProfile=zeros and empty skills/mcp for every agent
 * other than Claude. This script re-runs the (now agent-aware) extractor
 * against existing transcripts and overwrites only those three fields. NO
 * LLM calls — labels and other LLM-derived fields are already correct.
 *
 * Usage: pnpm exec tsx scripts/backfill-analysis-tool-metrics.ts [--limit=N] [--dry-run]
 *
 * Environment:
 *   DATABASE_URL  MySQL connection string (defaults to local Docker MySQL)
 *
 * Pattern mirrors api/scripts/backfill-search.ts (cursor pagination, MySQL
 * bootstrap, --dry-run / --limit flags). Differences: no Turbopuffer write
 * path, no GitHub fetch, narrower per-row scope (just re-extract metrics
 * from already-stored transcripts).
 */

import { Kysely, MysqlDialect } from "kysely"
import { createPool } from "mysql2"

import type { DB } from "../db/types"
import {
  extractToolMetricsFromSessions,
  type ParsedSessionForMetrics,
} from "../src/lib/analysis-queue"
import { loadCheckpointTranscript } from "../src/lib/checkpoint-transcript"
import type { Db } from "../src/lib/db/db-types"
import { getCheckpointRepoName } from "../src/lib/entire-settings"
import { createCheckpointsNamespace } from "../src/lib/planetscale/checkpoints"
import { createReposNamespace } from "../src/lib/planetscale/repos"
import type { SessionTranscript } from "../src/types"

const BATCH_SIZE = 500

export interface BackfillDeps {
  db: Kysely<DB>
  loadTranscript: (
    args: { repoId: string; checkpointId: string },
  ) => Promise<{ sessions: SessionTranscript[] }>
}

export async function runBackfill(
  deps: BackfillDeps,
  options: { max: number; dryRun: boolean },
): Promise<{ processed: number; skipped: number; updated: number }> {
  const { db, loadTranscript } = deps
  const { max, dryRun } = options

  let cursor: { repo_id: string; checkpoint_id: string } | null = null
  let processed = 0
  let skipped = 0
  let updated = 0

  while (processed < max) {
    let q = db
      .selectFrom("repo_checkpoint_analyses")
      .select(["repo_id", "checkpoint_id", "analysis_json"])
      .where("status", "=", "complete")
      .where("analysis_json", "is not", null)
      .orderBy("repo_id")
      .orderBy("checkpoint_id")
      .limit(BATCH_SIZE)

    if (cursor) {
      const c = cursor
      q = q.where(({ eb, or, and }) =>
        or([
          eb("repo_id", ">", c.repo_id),
          and([eb("repo_id", "=", c.repo_id), eb("checkpoint_id", ">", c.checkpoint_id)]),
        ]),
      )
    }

    const batch = await q.execute()
    if (batch.length === 0) break

    for (const row of batch) {
      processed++

      let analysis: Record<string, unknown>
      try {
        analysis =
          typeof row.analysis_json === "string"
            ? (JSON.parse(row.analysis_json) as Record<string, unknown>)
            : (row.analysis_json as Record<string, unknown>)
      } catch (err) {
        if (err instanceof SyntaxError) {
          skipped++
          console.warn(`skip repo=${row.repo_id} cp=${row.checkpoint_id}: ${err.message}`)
          continue
        }
        throw err
      }

      const loaded = await loadTranscript({
        repoId: row.repo_id,
        checkpointId: row.checkpoint_id,
      })
      if (loaded.sessions.length === 0) {
        skipped++
        continue
      }

      const sessions: ParsedSessionForMetrics[] = loaded.sessions.map((s) => ({
        agent: s.agent,
        messages: s.messages,
      }))
      const metrics = extractToolMetricsFromSessions(sessions)

      const updatedAnalysis = {
        ...analysis,
        toolProfile: metrics.toolProfile,
        skillsUsed: metrics.skillsUsed,
        mcpServersUsed: metrics.mcpServersUsed,
      }

      if (!dryRun) {
        await db
          .updateTable("repo_checkpoint_analyses")
          .set({ analysis_json: JSON.stringify(updatedAnalysis) })
          .where("repo_id", "=", row.repo_id)
          .where("checkpoint_id", "=", row.checkpoint_id)
          .execute()
        updated++
      }
    }

    cursor = {
      repo_id: batch[batch.length - 1]!.repo_id,
      checkpoint_id: batch[batch.length - 1]!.checkpoint_id,
    }
    console.log(
      `processed=${processed} skipped=${skipped} updated=${updated} cursor=${cursor.repo_id}/${cursor.checkpoint_id}`,
    )
  }

  return { processed, skipped, updated }
}

// --- CLI entry point (mirror of backfill-search.ts:createDb + main) ---

function createKysely(): Kysely<DB> {
  const url = process.env.DATABASE_URL ?? "REDACTED"
  const parsed = new URL(url)
  const isLocalhost = parsed.hostname === "localhost" || parsed.hostname === "127.0.0.1"
  return new Kysely<DB>({
    dialect: new MysqlDialect({
      pool: createPool({
        host: parsed.hostname,
        port: Number(parsed.port) || 3306,
        user: decodeURIComponent(parsed.username),
        password: decodeURIComponent(parsed.password),
        database: parsed.pathname.replace("/", ""),
        ssl: isLocalhost ? undefined : { rejectUnauthorized: true },
      }),
    }),
  })
}

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const kysely = createKysely()

  // Build a partial Db for loadCheckpointTranscript. It only reads
  // db.checkpoints (verified at checkpoint-transcript.ts:347, 417, 444),
  // and we look up `repos` per row for getCheckpointRepoName. Constructing
  // these directly avoids the Cloudflare-Worker getDb(env) factory.
  const db = {
    checkpoints: createCheckpointsNamespace(kysely),
    repos: createReposNamespace(kysely),
  } as Pick<Db, "checkpoints" | "repos">

  const loadTranscript: BackfillDeps["loadTranscript"] = async ({ repoId, checkpointId }) => {
    // Mirror analysis-queue.ts:289-298 (production dispatcher's lookup).
    const location = await db.checkpoints.findById(repoId, checkpointId, undefined)
    if (!location?.commit) return { sessions: [] }
    const repo = await db.repos.getById(repoId)
    if (!repo) return { sessions: [] }
    const repoName = getCheckpointRepoName(repo)
    const loaded = await loadCheckpointTranscript({
      db: db as Db,
      repoId,
      checkpointId,
      checkpoint: location.commit,
      checkpointRepoFullName: repoName,
      token: undefined,
    })
    return { sessions: loaded.sessions }
  }

  const limitFlag = process.argv.find((a) => a.startsWith("--limit="))?.split("=")[1]
  const max = limitFlag ? parseInt(limitFlag, 10) : Infinity
  const dryRun = process.argv.includes("--dry-run")

  const result = await runBackfill({ db: kysely, loadTranscript }, { max, dryRun })
  console.log(`done. ${JSON.stringify(result)}`)
  await kysely.destroy()
}

if (process.argv[1] && /backfill-analysis-tool-metrics\.ts$/.test(process.argv[1])) {
  main().catch((err) => {
    console.error(err)
    process.exit(1)
  })
}
```

The `db as Db` cast is intentional and minimal — `loadCheckpointTranscript` types its arg as `Db` but only reads `.checkpoints`.

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching fresh subagent per task, with two-stage review after each: spec compliance review first, then code quality review.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review (spec then quality) = high quality, fast iteration

## When to Use

```dot

    "Have implementation plan?" [shape=diamond];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" [shape=diamond];
    "Stay in this session?" [shape=diamond];
    "subagent-driven-development" [shape=box];
    "executing-plans" [shape=box];
    "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [shape=box];

    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Tasks mostly independent?" [label="yes"];
    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Stay in this session?" [label="yes"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no - tightly coupled"];
    "Stay in this session?" -> "subagent-driven-development" [label="yes"];
    "Stay in this session?" -> "executing-plans" [label="no - parallel session"];
}
```

**vs. Executing Plans (parallel session):**
- Same session (no context switch)
- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution)
- Two-stage review after each task: spec compliance first, then code quality
- Faster iteration (no human-in-loop between tasks)

## The Process

```dot

    rankdir=TB;

    subgraph cluster_per_task {
        label="Per Task";
        "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];

        "Implementer subagent implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" [shape=box];

        "Mark task complete in TodoWrite" [shape=box];
    }

    "Read plan, extract all tasks with full text, note context, create TodoWrite" [shape=box];
    "More tasks remain?" [shape=diamond];
    "Dispatch final code reviewer subagent for entire implementation" [shape=box];
    "Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch" [shape=box style=filled fillcolor=lightgreen];

    "Read plan, extract all tasks with full text, note context, create TodoWrite" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)";

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture, design, and review tasks**: use the most capable available model.

**Task complexity signals:**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## Handling Implementer Status

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Proceed to spec compliance review.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, escalate to the human

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

## Prompt Templates

- `./implementer-prompt.md` - Dispatch implementer subagent
- `./spec-reviewer-prompt.md` - Dispatch spec compliance reviewer subagent
- `./code-quality-reviewer-prompt.md` - Dispatch code quality reviewer subagent

```

## Advantages

**vs. Manual execution:**
- Subagents follow TDD naturally
- Fresh context per task (no confusion)
- Parallel-safe (subagents don't interfere)
- Subagent can ask questions (before AND during work)

**vs. Executing Plans:**
- Same session (no handoff)
- Continuous progress (no waiting)
- Review checkpoints automatic

**Efficiency gains:**
- No file reading overhead (controller provides full text)
- Controller curates exactly what context is needed
- Subagent gets complete information upfront
- Questions surfaced before work begins (not after)

**Quality gates:**
- Self-review catches issues before handoff
- Two-stage review: spec compliance, then code quality
- Review loops ensure fixes actually work
- Spec compliance prevents over/under-building
- Code quality ensures implementation is well-built

**Cost:**
- More subagent invocations (implementer + 2 reviewers per task)
- Controller does more prep work (extracting all tasks upfront)
- Review loops add iterations
- But catches issues early (cheaper than debugging later)

## Red Flags

**Never:**
- Start implementation on main/master branch without explicit user consent
- Skip reviews (spec compliance OR code quality)
- Proceed with unfixed issues
- Dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts)
- Make subagent read plan file (provide full text instead)
- Skip scene-setting context (subagent needs to understand where task fits)
- Ignore subagent questions (answer before letting them proceed)
- Accept "close enough" on spec compliance (spec reviewer found issues = not done)
- Skip review loops (reviewer found issues = implementer fixes = review again)
- Let implementer self-review replace actual review (both are needed)
- **Start code quality review before spec compliance is ✅** (wrong order)
- Move to next task while either review has open issues

**If subagent asks questions:**
- Answer clearly and completely
- Provide additional context if needed
- Don't rush them into implementation

**If reviewer finds issues:**
- Implementer (same subagent) fixes them
- Reviewer reviews again
- Repeat until approved
- Don't skip the re-review

**If subagent fails task:**
- Dispatch fix subagent with specific instructions
- Don't try to fix manually (context pollution)

In `api/scripts/backfill-analysis-tool-metrics.ts`, the `--limit=N` flag is checked only at the top of the `while` loop (`while (processed < max)`), but `processed++` happens per row inside the inner `for`. With `BATCH_SIZE=500` and `--limit=10`, the script actually processes 500 rows.

Operators commonly run `--limit=10 --dry-run` as a smoke test, expecting to see at most 10 rows. They'd see 500. This is a real foot-gun.

## Fix

Add an inner-loop break: inside the `for (const row of batch) { ... }` loop, immediately after `processed++`, add:

```ts
if (processed > max) {
  processed-- // un-count: we never actually started this row
  break
}
```

Wait — that's awkward. Cleaner shape:

```ts
for (const row of batch) {
  if (processed >= max) break
  processed++
  // ... rest of the loop body
}
```

The check goes BEFORE `processed++`. If `processed` is already at `max`, break before doing anything else.

Then add an outer-loop check that breaks once the inner loop broke due to max:

```ts
if (processed >= max) break
```

Add this right after the `for` loop closes, BEFORE the cursor advance / log statements. This way the cursor doesn't advance and we don't print a misleading "processed=X cursor=..." line for a batch we cut short.

There's a layered set of options from cheap → expensive. Recommendation: do steps 1-3 before merge (under 10 minutes), then 4 after merge as the production-reality check.

**1. Local dry-run smoke test** (zero risk — no writes)
```bash
cd api && DATABASE_URL=<dev-db-url> pnpm exec tsx scripts/backfill-analysis-tool-metrics.ts --dry-run --limit=20
```
Confirms the script bootstraps, paginates, and processes rows. Doesn't validate correctness — just shape.

**2. Targeted before/after on the known-broken Codex checkpoint** (the original signal)
That checkpoint we identified at the start of this thread (`7a9387cf9003`) is the load-bearing test case — it had all-zero `toolProfile` because of the old Claude-shaped extractor. Steps:
- Read its current `analysis_json` from the DB → confirm `toolProfile.categories.shell.count === 0`, `skillsUsed === []`
- Run the backfill targeting just that row (e.g., `--limit=1` after manually narrowing to its `(repo_id, checkpoint_id)`, or temporarily add a WHERE filter)
- Re-read `analysis_json` → confirm non-zero shell/fileOps counts and `mcpServersUsed` populated where applicable
- Verify other fields (`extraction.labels`, `total_transcript_tokens`) are unchanged

This is the only test that proves agent-aware classification works end-to-end against real production data.

**3. Idempotency check** — run the same `--limit=1` twice. Output should be identical the second time. Validates re-running the backfill is safe.

**4. Post-merge production spot check** — after deploy, hit `GET /api/v1/me/recap?timeframe=last-month` for an account with Codex activity. Inspect the per-agent row for Codex; `toolMix` and `mcpServers` should be populated. This is the user-visible verification.

**Tradeoff:** Step 2 requires either a non-prod DB with that checkpoint's data, or running the backfill against prod with `--limit=1`. The latter is low-blast-radius (single row, idempotent, only overwrites 3 fields) but is a prod write — wants explicit go-ahead.

# Setup

## 1. Install Dependencies

```bash
pnpm install
```

## 2. Configure Secrets

Install 1Password CLI and populate dev secrets from the shared vault:

```bash
brew install 1password-cli
```

```bash
mise run secrets
```

Secrets are stored in 1Password (Shared vault, item `entirehq/entire.io`).

<details>
<summary>Creating a new GitHub App (if needed)</summary>

1. Create at https://github.com/settings/apps/new
1. Callback URL: `http://localhost:8787/auth/github/callback`. Enable "Expire user authorization tokens", uncheck "Request user authorization (OAuth) during installation" and "Enable Device Flow"
1. Webhook URL needs to be accessible over public internet so use NGrok or something and should be `$host/api/v1/webhooks/github`
1. Repository permissions: Contents > Read-only
1. No event subscriptions; only allow on "this account" (your Github account)

</details>

## 3. Set Up MySQL (Local - Recommended)

We use a local MySQL Docker container for dev and tests.

**Prerequisites:** Docker must be installed and running. Choose one:

**Option A: Colima (lightweight, recommended for macOS)**

Colima is a free, open-source tool that runs Docker containers inside a lightweight Linux VM. It's recommended over Docker Desktop because it uses fewer resources and avoids Docker Desktop's commercial license requirements for larger organizations, but it's CLI-only with no GUI dashboard.

```bash
brew install colima docker docker-compose
colima start
```

**Option B: [Docker Desktop](https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/)**

**Option C: [OrbStack](https://orbstack.dev/)**

---

```bash
# Start local DB
mise run api-db-start

# Create DB and apply migrations
mise run api-db-reset

# To just run migrations (i.e., don't blow everything away)
mise run api-db-migrate
```

## 4. Run the Dev Server

```bash
mise run dev
```

The server will be accessible at `http://localhost:5173`.

## 5. PostHog (Analytics & Toolbar)

PostHog env vars are populated by `mise run secrets` into `frontend/.env` and `website/.env`.

To use the PostHog toolbar locally (inspect elements, heatmaps, feature flags), launch it from:
https://eu.posthog.com/project/102418/toolbar

The dev CSP in `vite.config.ts` allows both `42.entire.io` and `*.posthog.com` for the toolbar. Production routes everything through the `42.entire.io` proxy.

## 6. Configure Hyperdrive (Staging/Production)

Cloudflare Hyperdrive accelerates MySQL connections from Workers. First, in Planetscale, create a
password. It must be "admin" because it should be allowed to run DDL operations. Then, create a
Hyperdrive config for each environment:

```bash
# Staging (default wrangler env)
pnpm exec wrangler hyperdrive create entire-db-staging \
  --connection-string="REDACTED"

# Production
pnpm exec wrangler hyperdrive create entire-db-production \
  --connection-string="REDACTED"
```

Then update the Hyperdrive IDs in `api/wrangler.jsonc`:

- Default environment: replace `STAGING_HYPERDRIVE_ID` with the staging ID
- `env.production`: replace `PRODUCTION_HYPERDRIVE_ID` with the production ID

**Running migrations against staging/production:**

The migration runner uses `DATABASE_URL` to connect directly to PlanetScale (not via Hyperdrive, which is for Workers only). Get the connection string from the PlanetScale dashboard under your branch's connection settings.

## 7. Restore from a PlanetScale Backup

If you need to switch to a backup (e.g., after a bad migration):

1. Go to [PlanetScale backups](https://app.planetscale.com/entire/partial-to/backups) and pick one
2. Click "Restore to new branch" and pick a size (smallest is enough)
3. Stay on the page until the branch is ready
4. Go to [branches](https://app.planetscale.com/entire/partial-to/branches) and make the new branch the default
5. Click the new branch, then "Connect" (top right)
6. Generate new passwords:
   - For migrations: role must be **admin** (needs DDL)
   - For the Worker: **Read/Write** is enough
7. Update credentials in two places:

**Hyperdrive** (Worker connection): go to [Hyperdrive settings](https://dash.cloudflare.com/8b04592ed74a5cce30d355b07276caf3/workers/hyperdrive/e55646c03c454ba2a20ae7357c4b9f4b/settings). Hit the "Edit" button above the table (don't try to edit individual values).

**GitHub Actions** (migration runner): go to [action secrets](https://github.com/entirehq/entire.io/settings/secrets/actions) and update `PLANETSCALE_DATABASE_URL_PARTIAL`. The format is:

```
REDACTED
```

## 8. Deploy frontend changes to Staging

Staging access must be requested from a Cloudflare admin.

You can see a full list of deployments and logs in the [Cloudflare dashboard](https://dash.cloudflare.com/8b04592ed74a5cce30d355b07276caf3/pages/view/partial-to-frontend).

To kick off a staging deploy locally, run the following from the `frontend/` directory:

```bash
VITE_API_BASE_URL=https://partial.to pnpm run build && pnpm exec wrangler pages deploy dist --project-name=partial-to-frontend --branch=main
```

> **Why `--branch=main`?** Cloudflare Pages uses the branch name to determine which deployment is the "production" deployment for the project. The `partial-to-frontend` Pages project treats `main` as its production branch. If you pass your actual working branch name instead, Cloudflare will create a preview deployment at a different URL rather than updating the primary staging deployment. This is a Cloudflare Pages convention — `--branch=main` here refers to the Pages project's production branch, not your git branch.

## 7. Chrome DevTools MCP (Optional)

Lets Claude Code or Codex interact with a running Chrome instance — inspect pages, run performance traces, execute scripts, take screenshots.

**Prerequisites:** Chrome >= M144

1. In Chrome, navigate to `chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging` and allow incoming debugging connections
2. For Claude Code, `.mcp.json` already includes the `chrome-devtools` server
3. For Codex, `.codex/config.toml` already includes the `chrome-devtools` server for this project. If you prefer a per-user setup instead, run `codex mcp add chrome-devtools -- pnpm dlx chrome-devtools-mcp@latest --autoConnect --slim`
4. Trust the project in Codex if prompted, restart your client if it is already running, then test by asking it to check the performance of a URL

> **Note:** Chrome must be running before starting Claude Code or Codex. Connects to the default profile. A permission dialog is shown on first connection.

### Slim vs Full mode

The default config uses `--slim`, which exposes 3 core tools:

- **navigate** — load a URL
- **evaluate** — run JavaScript in page context
- **screenshot** — capture the page

This covers most dev tasks since `evaluate` can do almost anything programmatically, and keeps token usage low.
